question: What is the primary role of an Operating System?
option_a: Act as an intermediary between user/applications and computer hardware
option_b: Compile C++ code to machine instructions

question: Which component of the OS resides permanently in main memory (RAM)?
option_a: Kernel

question: What is a system call?
option_a: Programmatic request by user space application for services from kernel
option_b: A call between two user processes

question: Which mechanism switches execution CPU mode from User Mode to Kernel Mode?
option_a: Hardware Interrupt or Trap/Syscall

question: What is a Process Control Block (PCB)?
option_a: Data structure in kernel storing all information about a process (state, PC, registers, memory bounds)
option_b: A block of code inside process text segment

question: What state is a process in when it is waiting to be assigned to a processor by scheduler?
option_a: Ready State

question: What state is a process in when it is waiting for an I/O operation to complete?
option_a: Waiting / Blocked State

question: What is a thread in operating systems?
option_a: The smallest unit of CPU execution within a process
option_b: A separate process with independent address space

question: Threads belonging to the same process share which memory section?
option_a: Heap and Data / Code segments

question: Each thread in a multithreaded process has its own unique:
option_a: Stack frame and Registers / PC

question: What is context switching?
option_a: Saving state of currently running process/thread and restoring state of another process/thread
option_c: Moving process from RAM to Swap disk
option_d: Converting code from C to Assembly

question: Is context switching pure CPU overhead?
option_a: Yes, CPU performs no useful application work during context switch

question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm gives shortest average waiting time for a given set of processes?
option_a: Shortest Job First (SJF) / SRTF

question: What is the main drawback of Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling?
option_a: Difficulty in knowing or predicting length of next CPU burst in advance

question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm uses time quanta and circular queue, ideal for time-sharing systems?
option_a: Round Robin (RR)

question: What happens in Round Robin scheduling if the time quantum is extremely large?
option_a: It degenerates into First-Come First-Served (FCFS)

question: What is Convoy Effect in CPU scheduling?
option_a: Short processes waiting behind a long CPU-bound process in FCFS scheduling
option_b: Threads stalling due to lock contention

question: What is process starvation?
option_a: A process waiting indefinitely due to lower priority or scheduler bias
option_b: A process running out of RAM

question: How can process starvation be prevented in priority scheduling?
option_a: Aging (gradually increasing priority of processes waiting long)

question: What is a Race Condition?
option_a: Situation where concurrent output depends on executed order or timing of un-synchronized threads
option_b: Process running faster than CPU clock
option_d: Two processes finishing at exact same millisecond

question: What is a Critical Section in process synchronization?
option_a: Segment of code accessing shared resources that must not be concurrently accessed by multiple processes

question: What three criteria must any solution to critical section problem satisfy?
option_a: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting

question: What is a Semaphore?
option_a: An integer variable used for process synchronization accessed via wait() / P() and signal() / V() operations

question: What is the difference between Binary Semaphore and Mutex?
option_a: Mutex includes ownership (only locking thread can unlock); Binary Semaphore has no ownership concept
option_c: Semaphore is hardware; Mutex is software

question: What is a Deadlock in operating systems?
option_a: Set of processes blocked because each holds a resource and waits for another resource held by another process
option_b: A process stuck in infinite loop
option_c: A system crash due to power loss

question: What are the 4 necessary Coffman conditions for a Deadlock to occur?
option_a: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait

question: Which famous algorithm is used for Deadlock Avoidance in OS?
option_a: Banker's Algorithm

question: What does Banker's Algorithm check before allocating resources?
option_a: Whether allocating resources leaves system in a Safe State

question: What is a Safe State in deadlock avoidance?
option_a: A state where there exists at least one execution sequence allowing all processes to complete without deadlock

question: What are the 3 main approaches to handle deadlocks?
option_a: Deadlock Prevention/Avoidance, Detection & Recovery, or Ignoring (Ostrich algorithm)

question: What is Logical Address Space vs Physical Address Space?
option_a: Logical address is generated by CPU (virtual); Physical address is actual address loaded into memory unit (RAM)
option_b: Logical is disk space; Physical is RAM
option_c: Logical is register; Physical is cache

question: What hardware component translates Virtual/Logical addresses to Physical addresses at runtime?
option_a: Memory Management Unit (MMU)

question: What is Paging in memory management?
option_a: Memory management scheme dividing physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages

question: What is a Page Table?
option_a: Data structure maintained by OS for each process mapping virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers

question: What is Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
option_a: High-speed hardware memory cache storing recent page table translations to speed up MMU lookups
option_b: A secondary page table on SSD
option_d: A CPU register for stack pointer

question: What is Internal Fragmentation?
option_a: Unused allocated memory space inside an assigned page or block
option_b: Unused memory space between non-contiguous allocated blocks

question: What is External Fragmentation?
option_a: Total free memory is enough to satisfy request, but memory is non-contiguous, so allocation fails

question: How does Segmentation differ from Paging?
option_a: Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized logical units (code, stack, data); Paging uses fixed-size pages
option_b: Segmentation is hardware only; Paging is software
option_c: Paging causes external fragmentation; Segmentation causes none

question: What is Virtual Memory?
option_a: Technique allowing execution of processes that are not completely loaded into physical RAM
option_b: Memory stored on USB flash drives
option_c: RAM allocated for virtual machines only

question: What is Demand Paging?
option_a: Loading pages into RAM only when they are accessed/needed during execution
option_b: Loading entire process into RAM at start

question: What occurs when a process attempts to access a page that is not currently loaded in RAM?
option_a: Page Fault

question: What step occurs during Page Fault handling?
option_a: OS traps to kernel, locates page on disk/swap, finds free frame in RAM, loads page, and resumes instruction

question: What is Thrashing in virtual memory?
option_a: High paging activity where OS spends more time swapping pages in/out than executing process code
option_c: CPU running at 100% capacity on loops

question: What causes Thrashing?
option_a: Process size exceeding allocated frames such that sum of working sets > total physical memory

question: What is FIFO Page Replacement Algorithm?
option_a: Replaces the page that was brought into memory earliest
option_c: Replaces page that will not be used for longest time in future

question: What is Belady's Anomaly?
option_a: For some page replacement algorithms (like FIFO), page fault rate may increase when allocated frames increase
option_c: Virtual memory running out of space

question: Does Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement algorithm suffer from Belady's Anomaly?
option_a: No, LRU belongs to stack algorithms class which never suffers from Belady's Anomaly
option_c: Only when frame count is odd

question: What is the Optimal Page Replacement Algorithm (OPT)?
option_a: Replaces page that will not be used for longest duration in future (theoretical baseline)
option_d: Replaces page with highest dirty bit

question: What is a Dirty Bit (Modify Bit) in page table entry?
option_a: A flag indicating whether page has been modified since loaded into RAM, requiring write-back to disk
option_c: A bit locking page against reads

question: What is spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line)?
option_a: Data held in intermediate buffer/disk area enabling devices operating at different speeds to process data (e.g. print queue)

question: What is Direct Memory Access (DMA)?
option_a: Feature allowing I/O hardware devices to transfer data directly to/from RAM without continuous CPU intervention
option_b: CPU writing directly to video card
option_c: User app writing directly to disk sectors
option_d: Bypassing RAM to write to L1 cache

question: What is an Interrupt Vector Table (IVT)?
option_a: Array of memory addresses holding pointers to Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs)

question: What is a Trap in OS context?
option_a: A software-generated interrupt caused by error (e.g. divide by zero) or system call request

question: What is a File Allocation Table (FAT)?
option_a: File system structure mapping files to clusters on disk drive using a linked table

question: In UNIX file system, what is an inode?
option_a: Data structure storing metadata about a file (size, owner, permissions, block pointers) except filename
option_b: The physical disk block containing file text

question: What is symbolic link (symlink) vs hard link in UNIX?
option_a: Symlink points to file path; Hard link points directly to underlying inode number
option_b: Hard link works across different file systems; Symlink does not
option_c: Deleting target file breaks hard link but keeps symlink

question: What disk scheduling algorithm services disk requests in order they arrive?
option_a: FCFS (First-Come First-Served)

question: What disk scheduling algorithm selects request with minimum seek time from current head position?
option_a: SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First)

question: What is SCAN (Elevator) disk scheduling algorithm?
option_a: Disk head moves from one end of disk to other, servicing requests along way, then reverses direction
option_b: Head moves randomly servicing shortest requests
option_c: Head jumps back to start without servicing on return

question: What is C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) disk scheduling?
option_a: Head moves from one end to other servicing requests, then returns immediately to start without servicing on return trip
option_b: Services requests in circular ring buffer
option_c: Bounces back and forth like elevator

question: What is RAID 0?
option_a: Disk striping offering high performance but zero redundancy / fault tolerance

question: What is RAID 1?
option_a: Disk mirroring providing full data redundancy by duplicating data on two or more disks
option_b: Disk striping with no fault tolerance

question: What is RAID 5?
option_a: Block-level striping with distributed parity requiring at least 3 disks
option_c: Dedicated single parity disk with non-striped data

question: What is the minimum number of disks required for RAID 5?
What is RAID 10 (1+0)?
option_a: Combination of RAID 1 (mirroring) and RAID 0 (striping), offering high speed and fault tolerance

question: What is a Monolithic Kernel?
option_a: Kernel architecture where all OS services (filesystem, drivers, IPC, memory) run in single kernel address space
option_b: Kernel where each service runs as isolated user space process
option_c: A kernel designed for single-core CPUs only
option_d: A kernel stored in read-only BIOS memory

question: What is a Microkernel?
option_a: Kernel architecture keeping only minimum essential services (IPC, basic memory, scheduling) in kernel space; rest in user space
option_b: A monolithic kernel under 1 MB in size
option_c: A kernel running inside web browser

question: What is advantage of Microkernel over Monolithic Kernel?
option_a: Higher modularity, stability, and security (driver crash does not bring down entire kernel)
option_b: Faster execution speed due to zero IPC overhead

question: What is fork() system call in UNIX?
option_a: Creates a new child process which is an exact duplicate of calling parent process
option_b: Executes a new binary program in current process space

question: What value does fork() return to the parent process on success?
option_a: Process ID (PID) of the newly created child process

question: What value does fork() return to the newly created child process?
What is exec() family system call in UNIX?
option_a: Replaces current process image with a new process image loaded from an executable file

question: What is an Orphan Process in UNIX?
option_a: A process whose parent process has terminated, now adopted by init / systemd (PID 1)
option_b: A process that has finished execution but entry remains in process table
option_c: A process stuck in infinite wait

question: What is a Zombie Process in UNIX?
option_a: A process that has completed execution but whose exit status has not yet been read by parent via wait()
option_b: A process running on dead CPU core
option_c: A process causing high CPU usage

question: How do parent processes clean up zombie child processes?
option_a: By invoking wait() or waitpid() system call to read exit status

question: What is spinlock?
option_a: A lock where thread continuously loops (busily waits) checking if lock is available
option_b: A lock that sleeps thread immediately

question: When is a spinlock preferred over a sleeping lock?
option_a: When expected lock hold time is extremely short, avoiding context switch overhead
option_b: When lock will be held for hours

question: What is Priority Inversion?
option_a: Scenario where lower priority process holds resource needed by higher priority process, delaying high priority task
option_b: High priority process executing before low priority

question: How is Priority Inversion solved?
option_a: Priority Inheritance Protocol (low priority thread holding resource temporarily inherits high priority)

question: What is Readers-Writers Problem?
option_a: Classic synchronization problem where multiple readers can read concurrently, but writer requires exclusive access
option_b: Concurrency issue between CPU and disk
option_c: Deadlock between 2 threads writing to same file

question: What is Dining Philosophers Problem used to illustrate?
option_a: Synchronization challenges, deadlock, and resource starvation in concurrent systems

question: What is a Mutex?
option_a: Mutual exclusion lock allowing only one thread to hold lock and access critical section at a time

question: What is inter-process communication (IPC)?
option_a: Mechanisms provided by OS allowing independent processes to communicate and synchronize actions

question: What are common IPC mechanisms in operating systems?
option_a: Pipes, Named Pipes (FIFO), Message Queues, Shared Memory, and Sockets

question: Which IPC mechanism provides the fastest data exchange between processes on same machine?
option_a: Shared Memory (no system calls required during data transfer once mapped)

question: What is a Pipe in UNIX?
option_a: Unidirectional data channel allowing stdout of one process to connect to stdin of another process

question: What is copy-on-write (COW) during process creation (fork)?
option_a: Pages are shared between parent and child read-only; physical page copied only when either process writes to it
option_b: Copying full process memory during fork instantly
option_c: Writing data to swap space before RAM

question: What is a Memory Leak in operating systems?
option_a: Failure of a process to free dynamically allocated heap memory after use, reducing available RAM

question: What is overlay technique in memory management?
option_a: Keeps only instructions/data needed at a given time in memory, loading others over old ones as needed

question: What is Kernel Mode vs User Mode?
option_a: Kernel Mode has unrestricted access to hardware/instructions; User Mode has restricted access to protect system
option_b: Kernel mode is slower; User mode is faster
option_c: Kernel mode runs apps; User mode runs OS drivers
option_d: Kernel mode is 32-bit; User mode is 64-bit

question: What is a System Bootloader (e.g. GRUB)?
option_a: Initial program loaded from ROM/NVRAM that initializes hardware and loads OS kernel into RAM

question: What is BIOS / UEFI?
option_a: Firmware initializing hardware during boot process and launching bootloader

question: What is Thrashing Prevention Working-Set Model?
option_a: Tracks set of pages process actively referenced in recent time window to allocate sufficient frames

question: What is slab allocation in Linux kernel?
option_a: Memory management mechanism efficiently allocating small kernel data structures avoiding fragmentation

question: What is NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access)?
option_a: Multiprocessor architecture where memory access time depends on memory location relative to processor

question: What is real-time operating system (RTOS)?
option_a: OS designed to serve real-time applications processing data with minimal delay and strict deterministic deadlines
option_c: OS with high throughput graphical UI

question: What is Hard Real-Time vs Soft Real-Time system?
option_a: Hard real-time guarantees strict completion deadlines (failure is catastrophic); Soft real-time prioritizes deadlines but tolerates occasional delay
option_b: Hard is hardware-based; Soft is virtualized
option_c: Hard real-time runs on Linux; Soft on Windows

question: What is a Device Driver?
option_a: Specialized software module operating or controlling a particular hardware device attached to computer
option_d: An application for monitoring CPU temp

question: What is Context Switch Latency?
option_a: Time taken by OS kernel to stop one process/thread and resume another process/thread
option_b: Time to read file from SSD

question: What is an Operating System Shell?
option_a: User interface program that interprets commands and launches processes
